title: Why Some Nations Are Rich and Others Aren't
subtitle: Same geography, same resources, wildly different fortunes. The best answer isn't culture or climate — it's the rules of the game.
hook: Nogales, Arizona and Nogales, Mexico sit on the same desert, share ancestry, even a name — yet one is far richer than the other. The border is the only difference. Multiply that puzzle across the world and you get the biggest question in economic history: why are some nations rich and others poor? The most powerful answer is deceptively boring — **institutions**: the rules that decide who gets to build, own, and keep.

sections.heading: Inclusive vs. extractive
sections.body:
Economists Acemoglu and Robinson split institutions into two kinds. **Inclusive** ones spread power and opportunity: secure property rights, fair courts, open markets — so ordinary people invest and innovate because they'll keep the rewards. **Extractive** ones concentrate power and squeeze the many to enrich a few — so why build anything if it'll be seized?

Same people, same land: give them inclusive rules and they prosper; give them extractive ones and they stagnate. The rules, not the resources, do the heavy lifting.

sections.caption: The same population under different rules diverges: inclusive institutions invite investment; extractive ones smother it.

sections.label: Property rights are the quiet engine
sections.body: The single most underrated ingredient: if you're confident you'll keep what you build, you'll build. Secure, enforceable property rights (and courts that mean it) turn effort into investment. Where a strongman or a corrupt official can seize your work, people rationally stop trying — and a whole economy can idle on that fear alone.

sections.label: It's contested, to be fair
sections.body: The 'institutions rule everything' thesis is influential but debated — geography (Jared Diamond) and culture also clearly matter, and institutions themselves have deep historical roots. Most historians land on 'institutions are a huge factor, interacting with geography and history,' not a single silver bullet. Hold it as a powerful lens, not gospel.

sections.caption: Inclusive vs. extractive institutions — the 'Why Nations Fail' thesis in brief.

takeaways: Neighboring places with the same geography can diverge hugely — pointing at **rules**, not resources.
**Inclusive** institutions spread rights & opportunity → people invest and innovate.
**Extractive** institutions concentrate power → little reason to build, so stagnation.
**Secure property rights** may be the quiet engine: keep what you build, and you'll build.
It's a powerful lens, not the whole story — geography and culture matter too.

quiz.q: What best explains the Nogales (US vs Mexico) wealth gap?
options: Different institutions / rules on the two sides of the border
quiz.explain: Same geography and ancestry — the border (institutions) is the key difference.

options: It shares power and opportunity broadly
It concentrates power and wealth in a few, discouraging others from building
quiz.explain: Extractive rules squeeze the many for the few, killing incentives to invest.

quiz.q: CALLBACK + BOSS: The state (Day 5) can build inclusive OR extractive institutions. What determines which way prosperity goes?
options: Whether the rules let ordinary people keep the rewards of what they build (secure rights, fair courts)
quiz.explain: A state is just machinery; whether it invites or smothers investment depends on whether its rules are inclusive. Institutions are how the state's power turns into wealth — or doesn't.

tg_quiz.q: Two towns, same desert & ancestry, one much richer. Biggest reason?
tg_quiz.correct: Right — the rules of the game, not the resources.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's institutions — the rules people live under, not geography.
tg_quiz.explain: Inclusive rules invite investment; extractive ones smother it.
